claim: Whole-genome sequencing of 310 quinoa accessions revealed 2.9 million polymorphic high confidence single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) loci.
source: Whole-genome sequencing of 310 accessions revealed 2.9 million polymorphic high confidence single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) loci.
evidence: The abstract directly states the number of accessions sequenced and SNPs identified, representing primary findings from the study's sequencing data.

claim: Highland and Lowland quinoa were clustered into two main groups with FST divergence of 0.36.
source: Highland and Lowland quinoa were clustered into two main groups, with FST divergence of 0.36 and linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay of 6.5 and 49.8 kb, respectively.
evidence: The abstract presents FST values calculated from the sequencing data, representing a quantitative measure of population differentiation.

claim: Highland quinoa has linkage disequilibrium decay of 6.5 kb.
source: Highland and Lowland quinoa were clustered into two main groups, with FST divergence of 0.36 and linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay of 6.5 and 49.8 kb, respectively.
evidence: The LD decay value for Highland quinoa is directly stated based on analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Lowland quinoa has linkage disequilibrium decay of 49.8 kb.
source: Highland and Lowland quinoa were clustered into two main groups, with FST divergence of 0.36 and linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay of 6.5 and 49.8 kb, respectively.
evidence: The LD decay value for Lowland quinoa is directly stated based on analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: A genome-wide association study uncovered 600 SNPs stably associated with 17 traits.
source: A genome-wide association study using multi-year phenotyping trials uncovered 600 SNPs stably associated with 17 traits.
evidence: The abstract reports the number of stable SNP-trait associations identified from GWAS analysis of multi-year phenotypic data.

claim: Two candidate genes are associated with thousand seed weight.
source: Two candidate genes are associated with thousand seed weight, and a resistance gene analog is associated with downy mildew resistance.
evidence: The abstract states that candidate genes for thousand seed weight were identified from the GWAS results.

claim: A resistance gene analog is associated with downy mildew resistance.
source: Two candidate genes are associated with thousand seed weight, and a resistance gene analog is associated with downy mildew resistance.
evidence: The abstract reports identification of a resistance gene analog associated with downy mildew resistance from GWAS analysis.

claim: Pleiotropically acting loci for four agronomic traits important for adaptation were identified.
source: We also identified pleiotropically acting loci for four agronomic traits important for adaptation.
evidence: The abstract states that loci with pleiotropic effects on multiple agronomic traits were identified from the study.

claim: Climate change poses a great threat to crop production worldwide.
source: Climate change poses a great threat to crop production worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about climate change impacts on agriculture.

claim: In temperate climates of the world, higher temperatures and extended drought periods are expected.
source: In temperate climates of the world, higher temperatures and extended drought periods are expected.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about climate change projections for temperate regions.

claim: Quinoa was first domesticated about 5000–7000 years ago in the Andean region.
source: It was first domesticated about 5000–7000 years ago in the Andean region.
evidence: This is a historical statement about quinoa domestication that draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Quinoa was a staple food during the pre-Columbian era.
source: Quinoa was a staple food during the pre-Columbian era, and the cultivation declined after the introduction of crops like wheat and barley by the Spanish rulers.
evidence: This is a historical statement about quinoa's role in pre-Columbian societies based on established knowledge.

claim: Quinoa cultivation declined after the introduction of crops like wheat and barley by the Spanish rulers.
source: Quinoa was a staple food during the pre-Columbian era, and the cultivation declined after the introduction of crops like wheat and barley by the Spanish rulers.
evidence: This is a historical statement about changes in quinoa cultivation following Spanish colonization based on established knowledge.

claim: Quinoa can adapt to a broad range of agroecological regions due to diversity, biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, and ecological plasticity.
source: Owing to diversity, biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, and ecological plasticity, quinoa can adapt to a broad range of agroecological regions (González et al., 2015; Ruiz et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on quinoa's adaptability.

claim: The nutritional value of quinoa is higher than beef, fish, and other major cereals due to its high seed protein content and favorable amino acid composition.
source: Due to its high seed protein content and favorable amino acid composition, the nutritional value is even higher than beef, fish, and other major cereals (Abugoch James, 2009; Vega-Gálvez et al., 2010).
evidence: This nutritional comparison is supported by citations to previous research on quinoa's nutritional properties.

claim: A spontaneous hybridization event between two diploid species between 3.3 and 6.3 million years ago gave rise to the allotetraploid species quinoa.
source: A spontaneous hybridization event between two diploid species between 3.3 and 6.3 million years ago gave rise to the allotetraploid species quinoa (2n = 4x = 36) with a genome size of 1.45–1.5 Gb (nuclear DNA content 1C=1.49 pg) (Kolano et al., 2011; Palomino et al., 2008).
evidence: This evolutionary history is supported by citations to previous research on quinoa's origin.

claim: Quinoa is an allotetraploid species with 2n = 4x = 36 chromosomes.
source: A spontaneous hybridization event between two diploid species between 3.3 and 6.3 million years ago gave rise to the allotetraploid species quinoa (2n = 4x = 36) with a genome size of 1.45–1.5 Gb (nuclear DNA content 1C=1.49 pg) (Kolano et al., 2011; Palomino et al., 2008).
evidence: The chromosome number is stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Quinoa has a genome size of 1.45–1.5 Gb.
source: A spontaneous hybridization event between two diploid species between 3.3 and 6.3 million years ago gave rise to the allotetraploid species quinoa (2n = 4x = 36) with a genome size of 1.45–1.5 Gb (nuclear DNA content 1C=1.49 pg) (Kolano et al., 2011; Palomino et al., 2008).
evidence: The genome size is stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A reference genome of the coastal Chilean quinoa accession PI 614886 has been published with 44,776 predicted gene models.
source: A reference genome of the coastal Chilean quinoa accession PI 614886 has been published with 44,776 predicted gene models and whole-genome re-sequencing of Chenopodium pallidicaule and Chenopodium suecicum species, close relatives of the A and B subgenome donor species, respectively (Jarvis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement about the reference genome is supported by citation to the Jarvis et al., 2017 publication.

claim: The organellar genomes of quinoa are originated from the A-genome ancestor.
source: The organellar genomes are originated from the A-genome ancestor (Maughan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement about organellar genome origin is supported by citation to Maughan et al., 2019.

claim: Quinoa belongs to the Amaranthaceae family.
source: Quinoa belongs to the Amaranthaceae, together with some other economically important crops like sugar beet, red beet, spinach, and amaranth.
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification based on established botanical knowledge.

claim: Quinoa reproduces sexually after self-pollination.
source: It reproduces sexually after self-pollination.
evidence: This is a statement about quinoa's reproductive biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Quinoa accessions are typically homozygous inbred lines.
source: Quinoa accessions are typically homozygous inbred lines.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic structure of quinoa accessions based on established knowledge.

claim: Heterozygosity in some quinoa accessions has been reported, indicating cross-pollination.
source: Nonetheless, heterozygosity in some accessions has been reported, indicating cross-pollination (Christensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to Christensen et al., 2007.

claim: Routine protocols for F1 seed production in combination with marker-assisted selection have been developed recently in quinoa.
source: However, routine protocols for F1 seed production in combination with marker-assisted selection have been developed recently (Emrani et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement about breeding protocols is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: Systematic breeding of quinoa is still in its infancy compared to major crops.
source: Systematic breeding of quinoa is still in its infancy compared to major crops.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about quinoa breeding history based on established knowledge in crop breeding.

claim: Until recently, quinoa breeding has been mainly limited to Bolivia and Peru.
source: Until recently, breeding has been mainly limited to Bolivia (Gandarillas, 1979) and Peru (Bonifacio et al., 2013), the major growing quinoa areas.
evidence: This statement about the geographic distribution of quinoa breeding is supported by citations.

claim: Quinoa can be regarded as a partially domesticated crop.
source: Therefore, quinoa can be regarded as a partially domesticated crop.
evidence: This is an inference based on the short breeding history and presence of wild-type traits in quinoa.

claim: Many quinoa accessions suffer from seed shattering, branching, and non-appropriate plant height, typical domestication traits.
source: Many accessions suffer from seed shattering, branching, and non-appropriate plant height (PH), typical domestication traits.
evidence: This is an observation about phenotypic traits in quinoa accessions that reflects incomplete domestication.

claim: The major breeding objectives for quinoa are grain yield and seed size, downy mildew resistance, synchronized maturity, stalk strength, and low saponin content.
source: The major breeding objectives are apart from these characters: grain yield and seed size, downy mildew resistance, synchronized maturity, stalk strength, and low saponin content (Gomez‐Pando, 2015).
evidence: This statement about breeding objectives is supported by citation to Gomez-Pando, 2015.

claim: Activities have been intensified to breed quinoa genotypes adapted to temperate environments in Europe, North America, and China.
source: In the past years, activities have been intensified to breed quinoa genotypes adapted to temperate environments, for example, Europe, North America, and China (Murphy, 2018).
evidence: This statement about recent breeding activities is supported by citation to Murphy, 2018.

claim: The major problem for quinoa cultivation in temperate regions is adapting to long-day conditions because quinoa is predominantly a short-day plant.
source: Here, the major problem is adapting to long-day conditions because quinoa is predominantly a short-day plant due to its origin from regions near the equator.
evidence: This is a statement about photoperiod adaptation challenges based on quinoa's biology and geographic origin.

claim: Maughan et al., 2012, used five bi-parental populations to identify ca. 14,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
source: Maughan et al., 2012, used five bi-parental populations to identify ca. 14,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), from which 511 KASP markers were developed.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from a previous study by Maughan et al., 2012.

claim: 511 KASP markers were developed from SNPs identified by Maughan et al., 2012.
source: Maughan et al., 2012, used five bi-parental populations to identify ca. 14,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), from which 511 KASP markers were developed.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from a previous study by Maughan et al., 2012.

claim: Jarvis et al., 2017, re-sequenced 15 quinoa accessions and identified ca. 7.8 million SNPs.
source: Jarvis et al., 2017, re-sequenced 15 accessions and identified ca. 7.8 million SNPs.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from a previous study by Jarvis et al., 2017.

claim: Zhang et al., 2017, re-sequenced 11 quinoa accessions and identified 8 million SNPs and ca. 842,000 indels.
source: In another study, 11 quinoa accessions were re-sequenced, and 8 million SNPs and ca. 842,000 indels were identified (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from a previous study by Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: The diversity panel comprises 310 quinoa accessions representing regions of major geographical distributions of quinoa.
source: We assembled a diversity panel made of 310 quinoa accessions representing regions of major geographical distributions of quinoa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the composition of the study's diversity panel, with reference to a figure showing geographic distribution.

claim: The diversity panel includes 14 accessions from a previous study, of which 7 are wild relatives.
source: We included 14 accessions from a previous study, of which 7 are wild relatives (Jarvis et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the inclusion of previously sequenced accessions in the current study.

claim: The mean mapped read depth ranged from 4.07 to 14.55, with an average of 7.78.
source: The mean mapped read depth ranged from 4.07 to 14.55, with an average of 7.78, indicating an adequate mapping quality required for accurate SNP calling despite the relatively modest sequencing depth.
evidence: This reports sequencing depth statistics from the study's data.

claim: 45,330,710 unfiltered SNPs were identified by mapping sequence reads to the reference genome V2.
source: We mapped sequence reads to the reference genome V2 (CoGe id60716). Using mapping reads, we identified 45,330,710 unfiltered SNPs.
evidence: This reports the initial number of SNPs identified before filtering.

claim: After filtering, 4.5 million SNPs were identified in total for the base SNP set.
source: After filtering the initial set of SNPs, we identified 4.5 million SNPs in total for the base SNP set.
evidence: This reports the number of SNPs after initial filtering steps.

claim: The average SNP density across the whole genome was 2.39 SNPs/kb.
source: Across the whole genome, the average SNP density was 2.39 SNPs/kb.
evidence: This reports the calculated average SNP density from the study's data.

claim: SNP densities ranged from 0 to 122 SNPs/kb across genomic regions.
source: However, SNP densities were highly variable between genomic regions and ranged from 0 to 122 SNPs/kb (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports the range of SNP density variation observed in the data, with reference to a figure.

claim: No significant differences in SNP density were observed between the two subgenomes (A subgenome 2.43 SNPs/kb; B subgenome 2.35 SNPs/kb).
source: We did not observe significant differences in SNP density between the two subgenomes (a subgenome 2.43 SNPs/kb; B subgenome 2.35 SNPs/kb).
evidence: This reports a comparison of SNP density between subgenomes based on the study's data.

claim: No correlation was observed between sequencing depth and heterozygosity.
source: Moreover, we did not see any correlation between sequencing depth and heterozygosity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), which indicates an adequate mapping quality required for accurate SNP calling.
evidence: This reports an analysis of the relationship between sequencing depth and heterozygosity, with reference to a figure.

claim: Mean genotype quality (GQ) of heterozygous SNP calls was 61.34.
source: Mean GQ of the heterozygous SNP calls was 61.34, whereas the mean GQ of homozygous SNP calls was 21.19, indicating that a higher stringency was used for the heterozygous SNP calls.
evidence: This reports quality metrics for SNP calls from the study's data.

claim: Mean genotype quality (GQ) of homozygous SNP calls was 21.19.
source: Mean GQ of the heterozygous SNP calls was 61.34, whereas the mean GQ of homozygous SNP calls was 21.19, indicating that a higher stringency was used for the heterozygous SNP calls.
evidence: This reports quality metrics for SNP calls from the study's data.

claim: 598,383 SNPs were located upstream (within 5 kb from the transcript start site) of a gene.
source: Among SNPs located in non-coding regions, 598,383 and 617,699 SNPs were located upstream (within 5 kb from the transcript start site) and downstream (within 5 kb from the stop site) of a gene, whereas 114,654 and 251,481 SNPs were located within exon and intron sequences, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This reports the distribution of SNPs by genomic location, with reference to Table 1.

claim: 617,699 SNPs were located downstream (within 5 kb from the stop site) of a gene.
source: Among SNPs located in non-coding regions, 598,383 and 617,699 SNPs were located upstream (within 5 kb from the transcript start site) and downstream (within 5 kb from the stop site) of a gene, whereas 114,654 and 251,481 SNPs were located within exon and intron sequences, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This reports the distribution of SNPs by genomic location, with reference to Table 1.

claim: 114,654 SNPs were located within exon sequences.
source: Among SNPs located in non-coding regions, 598,383 and 617,699 SNPs were located upstream (within 5 kb from the transcript start site) and downstream (within 5 kb from the stop site) of a gene, whereas 114,654 and 251,481 SNPs were located within exon and intron sequences, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This reports the distribution of SNPs by genomic location, with reference to Table 1.

claim: 251,481 SNPs were located within intron sequences.
source: Among SNPs located in non-coding regions, 598,383 and 617,699 SNPs were located upstream (within 5 kb from the transcript start site) and downstream (within 5 kb from the stop site) of a gene, whereas 114,654 and 251,481 SNPs were located within exon and intron sequences, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This reports the distribution of SNPs by genomic location, with reference to Table 1.

claim: 70,604 missense SNPs were found within coding regions.
source: We found 70,604 missense SNPs and 41,914 synonymous SNPs within coding regions of 53,042 predicted gene models.
evidence: This reports the number of missense SNPs identified in the study's data.

claim: 41,914 synonymous SNPs were found within coding regions.
source: We found 70,604 missense SNPs and 41,914 synonymous SNPs within coding regions of 53,042 predicted gene models.
evidence: This reports the number of synonymous SNPs identified in the study's data.

claim: Across the whole genome, linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay between SNPs averaged 32.4 kb (at r2=0.2).
source: Across the whole genome, linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay between SNPs averaged 32.4 kb (at r2=0.2).
evidence: This reports the calculated LD decay distance from the study's data.

claim: No substantial LD differences were observed between subgenome A (r2=0.2 at 31.9 kb) and subgenome B (r2=0.2 at 30.7 kb).
source: We did not observe substantial LD differences between subgenome A (r2=0.2 at 31.9 kb) and subgenome B (r2=0.2 at 30.7 kb) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This reports a comparison of LD decay between subgenomes, with reference to a figure.

claim: Chromosome Cq6B exhibited a substantially slower LD decay compared to other chromosomes.
source: The magnitude of LD decay among chromosomes did not vary drastically except for chromosome Cq6B, which exhibited a substantially slower LD decay (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a b).
evidence: This reports an observation about LD decay on a specific chromosome, with reference to a figure.

claim: The first and second principal components (PC1(SNP) and PC2(SNP)) explained 23.35% and 9.45% of the variation, respectively.
source: The first and second principal components (PC1(SNP) and PC2(SNP)) explained 23.35% and 9.45% of the variation, respectively (Figure 1a)
evidence: This reports the variance explained by principal components from PCA analysis, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: 202 (66.67%) accessions were assigned to subpopulation 1 (SP1) and 101 (33.33%) to subpopulation 2 (SP2).
source: 202 (66.67%) accessions were assigned to subpopulation 1 (SP1) and 101 (33.33%) to subpopulation 2 (SP2).
evidence: This reports the distribution of accessions into subpopulations based on PCA analysis.

claim: SP1 comprised mostly Highland accessions, whereas Lowland accessions were found in SP2.
source: SP1 comprised mostly Highland accessions, whereas Lowland accessions were found in SP2.
evidence: This describes the geographic composition of the identified subpopulations.

claim: PCA demonstrated a higher genetic diversity of the Highland population.
source: PCA demonstrated a higher genetic diversity of the Highland population (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Two chromosomes, Cq6B and Cq8B, showed three distinct clusters in chromosome-specific PCA.
source: Nevertheless, two chromosomes, Cq6B and Cq8B, showed three distinct clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This reports an observation from chromosome-specific PCA analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Gene introgressions on chromosomes Cq6B and Cq8B from another interfertile group might have caused clustering differences.
source: We reasoned that gene introgressions on these two chromosomes from another interfertile group might have caused these differences.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed clustering pattern on specific chromosomes.

claim: The nucleotide diversity of the Highland population (5.78 × 10–4) was 1.62-fold higher compared to the Lowland population (3.56 × 10–4).
source: The nucleotide diversity of the Highland population (5.78 × 10–4) was 1.62-fold higher compared to the Lowland population (3.56 × 10–4) (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This reports calculated nucleotide diversity values for the two populations, with reference to Table 1 and a figure.

claim: The Lowland population showed a left-skewed distribution and negative Tajima's D value (–0.3883) indicating recent population growth.
source: We observed left-skewed distribution and negative Tajima's D value (–0.3883) in the Lowland populations indicating recent population growth (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This reports Tajima's D values and interprets them in terms of population history, with reference to Table 1 and a figure.

claim: The FST value between Highland and Lowland populations was estimated to be 0.36, illustrating strong population differentiation.
source: The FST value between populations was estimated to be 0.36, illustrating strong population differentiation.
evidence: This reports the calculated FST value and interprets it as indicating strong differentiation.

claim: Exonic SNPs are substantially higher in the Highland population compared to the Lowland population.
source: Concerning the regions of variants, exonic SNPs are substantially higher in the Highland population (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This reports a comparison of exonic SNP distribution between populations, with reference to Table 1 and a figure.

claim: 936 candidate genes were located within critical regions from the nucleotide diversity ratio analysis.
source: We identified 936, 953, and 546 candidate genes located within critical regions from the nucleotide diversity ratio (π (Highland/Lowland)), FST, and local PCA corner 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 9h).
evidence: This reports the number of candidate genes identified from different analyses, with reference to a figure.

claim: 953 candidate genes were located within critical regions from the FST analysis.
source: We identified 936, 953, and 546 candidate genes located within critical regions from the nucleotide diversity ratio (π (Highland/Lowland)), FST, and local PCA corner 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 9h).
evidence: This reports the number of candidate genes identified from different analyses, with reference to a figure.

claim: 546 candidate genes were located within critical regions from local PCA corner 1.
source: We identified 936, 953, and 546 candidate genes located within critical regions from the nucleotide diversity ratio (π (Highland/Lowland)), FST, and local PCA corner 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 9h).
evidence: This reports the number of candidate genes identified from different analyses, with reference to a figure.

claim: Only four genes were shared among all three analyses (nucleotide diversity ratio, FST, and local PCA corner 1).
source: Of these, only four genes were shared among all analyses, and 30 genes were shared between FST and genomic regions in corner 1 of the local PCA plot.
evidence: This reports the overlap of candidate genes identified by different analytical approaches.

claim: 30 genes were shared between FST and genomic regions in corner 1 of the local PCA plot.
source: Of these, only four genes were shared among all analyses, and 30 genes were shared between FST and genomic regions in corner 1 of the local PCA plot.
evidence: This reports the overlap of candidate genes identified by different analytical approaches.

claim: Genomic regions in corner 3 of the local PCA plot and with a high nucleotide diversity ratio shared 102 genes.
source: Genomic regions in corner 3 of the local PCA plot and with a high nucleotide diversity ratio shared 102 genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 9i).
evidence: This reports the overlap of candidate genes identified by different analytical approaches, with reference to a figure.

claim: 13 qualitative and 4 dichotomous traits were evaluated on 350 accessions across 2 different years.
source: We evaluated 13 qualitative and 4 dichotomous traits on 350 accessions across 2 different years.
evidence: This describes the phenotyping experiment conducted in the study.

claim: At the time of the final harvest, 254 accessions did not yet reach maturity (senescence).
source: At the time of the final harvest, 254 accessions did not yet reach maturity (senescence).
evidence: This reports an observation from the phenotyping experiment.

claim: All accessions produced seeds.
source: However, all accessions produced seeds, therefore they could be investigated for seed-related traits.
evidence: This reports an observation from the phenotyping experiment.

claim: High heritabilities were calculated for all quantitative traits except for the number of branches (NoB) and stem lying (STL).
source: High heritabilities were calculated for all quantitative traits except for the number of branches (NoB) and stem lying (STL), which indicates that the phenotypic variation between the accessions is caused mainly by genetic variation (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This reports heritability estimates from the phenotypic data, with reference to supplementary file.

claim: The strongest positive correlation was found between days to maturity (DTM) and panicle length (PL), and plant height (PH).
source: We found the strongest positive correlation between days to maturity (DTM) and panicle length (PL), and PH, whereas the strongest negative correlation was found between DTM and thousand seed weight (TSW) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports correlations calculated from the phenotypic data, with reference to a figure.

claim: The strongest negative correlation was found between DTM and thousand seed weight (TSW).
source: We found the strongest positive correlation between days to maturity (DTM) and panicle length (PL), and PH, whereas the strongest negative correlation was found between DTM and thousand seed weight (TSW) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports correlations calculated from the phenotypic data, with reference to a figure.

claim: The first two PCs of phenotype-based PCA explained 62.12% of the phenotypic variation between the accessions.
source: The first two PCs explained 62.12% of the phenotypic variation between the accessions.
evidence: This reports the variance explained by principal components from phenotype-based PCA.

claim: Most Lowland accessions were high yielding with high TSW and dense panicles.
source: PCA(PHEN) variables factor map indicated that most Lowland accessions were high yielding with high TSW and dense panicles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phenotype-based PCA results.

claim: Lowland accessions are early flowering and early maturing, and they are short.
source: Moreover, these accessions are early flowering and early maturing, and they are short (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phenotype-based PCA results, with reference to a figure.

claim: Lowland accessions are better adapted/selected for cultivation in long-day photoperiods than the Highland accessions.
source: Phenotype-based PCA(PHEN) also showed that the Lowland accessions are better adapted/selected for cultivation in long-day photoperiods than the Highland accessions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic characteristics observed in Lowland accessions.

claim: 294 accessions shared re-sequencing information and phenotypes out of 350 phenotypically evaluated accessions.
source: In total, 294 accessions shared the re-sequencing information and phenotypes out of 350 phenotypically evaluated accessions.
evidence: This reports the overlap between sequenced and phenotyped accessions used for GWAS.

claim: 1480 significant SNP-trait associations (MTAs) were identified for 17 traits.
source: In total, we identified 1480 significant (suggestive threshold: p<9.41e-7) SNP-trait associations (marker-trait association [MTAs]) for 17 traits (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This reports the total number of significant associations identified in the GWAS analysis.

claim: The number of MTAs ranged from 4 (STL) to 674 (DTM).
source: The number of MTAs ranged from 4 (STL) to 674 (DTM) (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This reports the range of MTAs identified for different traits, with reference to supplementary file.

claim: 600 consistent MTAs were identified across 11 traits.
source: We identified 600 consistent MTAs across 11 traits.
evidence: This reports the number of MTAs that were consistent across both years of the study.

claim: TSW and DTM showed the highest number of 'consistent' associations.
source: TSW and DTM showed the highest number of 'consistent' associations.
evidence: This reports which traits had the most consistent associations across years.

claim: Among consistent MTAs, 143 MTAs are located within a gene, and 22 SNPs resulted in a missense mutation.
source: Among these, 143 MTAs are located within a gene, and 22 SNPs resulted in a missense mutation (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This reports the functional annotation of consistent MTAs, with reference to supplementary file.

claim: MTAs for the duration from bolting to flowering, number of branching, seed yield, STL, and growth type (GT) were not 'consistent' between years.
source: MTAs for the duration from bolting to flowering (days to bolting to days to flowering), number of branching, seed yield, STL, and growth type (GT) were not 'consistent' between years (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This reports which traits did not show consistent associations across years, with reference to source data.

claim: Two genes (CqCYP76AD1 and CqDODA1) in the region 69.72–69.76 Mb on chromosome Cq1B exhibit high sequence homology to betalain synthesis pathway genes from sugar beet.
source: We identified highly significant MTAs for stem color on chromosome Cq1B (69.72–69.76 Mb). Two genes (CqCYP76AD1 and CqDODA1) in this region exhibit high sequence homology to betalain synthesis pathway genes BvCYP76AD1 (Hatlestad et al., 2012) and BvDODA1 (Bean et al., 2018) from sugar beet (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports candidate genes for stem color identified through GWAS and sequence homology analysis, with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: A significant MTA for saponin content on chromosome Cq5B between 8.85 and 9.2 Mb included 29 genes, of which two BHLH25 genes were in LD with the significantly associated SNPs.
source: A significant MTA for saponin content on chromosome Cq5B between 8.85 and 9.2 Mb included 29 genes, of which the two BHLH25 were in LD with the significantly associated SNPs.
evidence: This reports candidate genes for saponin content identified through GWAS analysis.

claim: BHLH25 genes were reported to control saponin content in quinoa.
source: BHLH25 genes were reported to control saponin content in quinoa (Jarvis et al., 2017; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jarvis et al., 2017 and reference to a figure.

claim: Seven MTAs on chromosome Cq2A were obtained with the traits days to flowering, DTM, PH, and PL indicating pleiotropic gene action.
source: We obtained seven MTAs on chromosome Cq2A with the traits days to flowering, DTM, PH, and PL indicating pleiotropic gene action (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This reports MTAs showing pleiotropic effects, with reference to Figure 3a and supplementary file.

claim: 89.94% of the variation in cross-phenotypes could be explained by the first two PCs.
source: We found 89.94% of the variation could be explained by the first two PCs of the cross-phenotypes (PCA(CP)) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This reports the variance explained by PCA of cross-phenotypes, with reference to a figure.

claim: 468 MTAs (PC1: 426 and PC2: 42) were identified across the whole genome in PC-GWAS.
source: We identified strong associations on chromosomes Cq2A, Cq7B (PC1), and Cq8B (PC2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). Of 468 MTAs (PC1: 426 and PC2: 42) across the whole genome, 222 (PC1: 211 and PC2: 11) are located within 95 annotated genes.
evidence: This reports the number of MTAs identified in PC-GWAS analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: 222 MTAs (PC1: 211 and PC2: 11) are located within 95 annotated genes in PC-GWAS.
source: Of 468 MTAs (PC1: 426 and PC2: 42) across the whole genome, 222 (PC1: 211 and PC2: 11) are located within 95 annotated genes.
evidence: This reports the number of MTAs located within genes from PC-GWAS analysis.

claim: 14 SNPs changed the amino acid sequence in 12 predicted protein sequences of associated genes in PC-GWAS.
source: We found 14 SNPs that changed the amino acid sequence in 12 predicted protein sequences of associated genes (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This reports the number of missense mutations in genes associated with cross-phenotypes, with reference to supplementary file.

claim: 605 genes were identified within 50 kb flanking MTAs (PC1: 520 and PC2: 85).
source: Altogether, 605 genes were identified (PC1: 520 and PC2: 85) (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This reports the number of genes identified near significant MTAs, with reference to supplementary file.

claim: The most significant SNP in the region 8.05–8.15 Mb on chromosome Cq2A is located within the CqGLX2-2 gene.
source: We found the region 8.05–8.15 Mb on chromosome Cq2A to be of special interest because it displays stable pleiotropic MTAs for days to flowering, DTM, PH, and PL. We identified five genes within this region and three of these were without known functions. The most significant SNP is located within the CqGLX2-2 gene, which encodes an enzyme of the glyoxalase family (Figure 3).
evidence: This reports the location of the most significant SNP and the gene it resides in, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The allele carrying a cytosine at the position with the most significant SNP is associated with early flowering, maturing, and short panicles and plants.
source: The allele carrying a cytosine at the position with the most significant SNP is associated with early flowering, maturing, and short panicles and plants (Figure 3b).
evidence: This reports the phenotypic effects of different alleles at the significant SNP, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: A strong MTA for thousand seed weight was found between 63.2 and 64.87 Mb on chromosome Cq8B.
source: We found a strong MTA between 63.2 and 64.87 Mb on chromosome Cq8B.
evidence: This reports the location of a significant MTA for thousand seed weight.

claim: Significantly associated SNPs for thousand seed weight were localized within two genes on chromosome Cq8B: one with homology to PP2C and one encoding a RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Significantly associated SNPs were localized within two genes (Figure 4). One gene displays homology to PP2C, encoding a member of the phosphatase-2C (PP2C) family protein and the second gene encodes a member of the RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase family.
evidence: This reports candidate genes for thousand seed weight identified through GWAS, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: PP2C and RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase genes were found to be involved in controlling seed size in soybean, maize, rice, and Arabidopsis.
source: These genes were found to be involved in controlling seed size in soybean, maize, rice, soybean, and Arabidopsis (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Five haplotypes were identified for CqPP2C gene.
source: We then checked haplotype variation and identified five and seven haplotypes for CqPP2C and CqRING genes, respectively.
evidence: This reports the number of haplotypes identified for the CqPP2C gene.

claim: Seven haplotypes were identified for CqRING gene.
source: We then checked haplotype variation and identified five and seven haplotypes for CqPP2C and CqRING genes, respectively.
evidence: This reports the number of haplotypes identified for the CqRING gene.

claim: Accessions carrying PP2C_hap3 and RING_hap7 displayed larger seeds in both years.
source: Accessions carrying PP2C_hap3 and RING_hap7 displayed larger seeds in both years (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports the phenotypic effects of specific haplotypes, with reference to figures.

claim: The most significant SNPs for downy mildew resistance are located in subgenome A.
source: Notably, our GWAS identified strong MTA for resistance against this disease. The most significant SNPs are located in subgenome A (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This reports the genomic location of SNPs associated with downy mildew resistance, with reference to source data.

claim: The A-genome progenitor seems to be the donor of downy mildew resistance.
source: Thus, the A-genome progenitor seems to be the donor of downy mildew resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of resistance-associated SNPs in subgenome A.

claim: A candidate gene within region 38.99–39.03 Mb on chromosome Cq2A encodes a protein with an NBS-LRR domain.
source: In addition, we identified a candidate gene within a region 38.99–39.03 Mb on chromosome Cq2A, which showed the highest significant association (Figure 3—source data 4). This gene encodes a protein with an NBS-LRR (nucleotide-binding site leucine-rich repeat) domain often found in resistance gene analogs with a function against mildew infection (Zhang et al., 2019a).
evidence: This reports a candidate gene for downy mildew resistance, with citation and reference to source data.

claim: NBS-LRR domain is often found in resistance gene analogs with a function against mildew infection.
source: This gene encodes a protein with an NBS-LRR (nucleotide-binding site leucine-rich repeat) domain often found in resistance gene analogs with a function against mildew infection (Zhang et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement about NBS-LRR domain function is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019a.

claim: The high genetic diversity and rapid LD breakdown in quinoa reflect the short breeding history of this crop.
source: The high genetic diversity and rapid LD breakdown reflect the short breeding history of this crop.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic diversity and LD results in the context of breeding history.

claim: Low or absent phenotypic variation within accessions demonstrates homogeneity as expected for a self-pollinating species.
source: Moreover, low or absent phenotypic variation within accessions demonstrates homogeneity as expected for a self-pollinating species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of phenotypic observations in the context of quinoa's reproductive biology.

claim: Over 16,000 accessions of quinoa are stored ex situ in seed banks in more than 30 countries.
source: Today, over 16,000 accessions of quinoa are stored ex situ in seed banks in more than 30 countries (Rojas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement about quinoa germplasm collections is supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2015.

claim: LD decay in quinoa (32.4 kb) is faster than in most studies with major crop species.
source: LD decay in quinoa (32.4 kb) is faster than in most studies with major crop species, for example, rapeseed (465.5 kb) (Wu et al., 2019), foxtail millet (Setaria italica, 100 kb) (Jia et al., 2013), pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan, 70 kb) (Varshney et al., 2017a), soybean (150 kb) (Zhou et al., 2015), and rice (200 kb) (Mather et al., 2007).
evidence: This comparison of LD decay across crops is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cross-pollination rates in some quinoa accessions can be up to 17.36%.
source: However, cross-pollination rates in some accessions can be up to 17.36% (Silvestri and Gil, 2000)
evidence: This statement about cross-pollination rates is supported by citation to Silvestri and Gil, 2000.

claim: The estimated FST value from this study (0.36) is in the similar range of FST estimates in rice subspecies indica and japonica (0.55).
source: The estimated FST value from this study (0.36) is in the similar range of FST estimates in rice subspecies indica and japonica (0.55) (Huang et al., 2010) and melon (Cucumis melo) subspecies melo and agrestis (0.46) (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison of FST values is supported by citations to studies on rice and melon.

claim: Two hypotheses have been proposed for the domestication of quinoa from C. hircinum: (1) one event that gave rise to Highland quinoa and subsequently to Lowland quinoa and (2) two separate domestication events giving rise to Highland and Lowland quinoa independently.
source: Two hypotheses have been proposed for the domestication of quinoa from C. hircinum: (1) one event that gave rise to Highland quinoa and subsequently to Lowland quinoa and (2) two separate domestication events giving rise to Highland and Lowland quinoa independently (Jarvis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement about domestication hypotheses is supported by citation to Jarvis et al., 2017.

claim: The study does not follow the second hypothesis (two separate domestication events) because C. hircinum accession BYU 566 was basal to both clades of the phylogenetic tree.
source: However, our study does not follow the second hypothesis because C. hircinum accession BYU 566 was basal to both clades of the phylogenetic tree (Highland and Lowland).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis results.

claim: Three possible scenarios are proposed to explain significant differences in LD structure, nucleotide diversity, Tajima's D and FST: (1) two independent domestication events with a substantial bottleneck on Lowland populations, (2) single domestication but strong population growth after adaptation of Lowland quinoa, or (3) strong adaptive selection after domestication.
source: Therefore, we propose three possible scenarios to explain significant differences in LD structure, nucleotide diversity, Tajima's D and FST: (1) two independent domestication events with a substantial bottleneck on Lowland populations, (2) single domestication but strong population growth after adaptation of Lowland quinoa, or (3) strong adaptive selection after domestication.
evidence: These are speculative scenarios proposed to explain the observed genetic patterns.

claim: The non-functional allele of soybean PP2C1 is associated with small seeds.
source: The non-functional allele of soybean PP2C1 is associated with small seeds (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement about soybean PP2C1 function is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2017.

claim: Downy mildew is the most acute disease for quinoa, caused by the fungus Peronospora variabili.
source: Downy mildew is the most acute disease for quinoa, caused by the fungus Peronospora variabili (Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement about downy mildew is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2010.

claim: A recent study attempted the identification of genes for downy mildew resistance based on GWAS analysis in quinoa but found no significant associations, probably due to the lack of power because of the low number of accessions used (61 and 88).
source: A recent study attempted the identification of genes based on a GWAS analysis in quinoa. However, no significant associations were found, probably due to the lack of power because of the low number of accessions used (61 and 88) (Colque-Little et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from a previous study by Colque-Little et al., 2021.

claim: Genes involved in the flowering time pathway have been shown to have pleiotropic effects.
source: Genes involved in the flowering time pathway have been shown to have pleiotropic effects (Auge et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement about flowering time genes is supported by citation to Auge et al., 2019.

claim: GLX genes have impacted cell division and proliferation in Amaranthus paniculatus.
source: GLX genes, among other functions, have impacted cell division and proliferation in Amaranthus paniculatus (Chakravarty and Sopory, 1998).
evidence: This statement about GLX gene function is supported by citation to Chakravarty and Sopory, 1998.

claim: 48 accessions are attractive as crossing partners for breeding programs because they are insensitive to photoperiod or long-day responsive.
source: Nevertheless, 48 accessions are attractive as crossing partners for breeding programs because they are insensitive to photoperiod or long-day responsive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phenotypic data in the context of breeding applications.

claim: Seeds were sown in the second week of April in 35× multi-tray pots.
source: Seeds were sown in the second week of April in 35× multi-tray pots.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the field experiment.

claim: Plants were transplanted to the field in the first week of May as single-row plots in a randomized complete block design with three blocks.
source: Then, plants were transplanted to the field in the first week of May as single-row plots in a randomized complete block design with three blocks.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the field trial.

claim: The distances between rows and between plants were set to 60 and 20 cm, respectively.
source: The distances between rows and between plants were set to 60 and 20 cm, respectively.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the field experiment.

claim: Each row plot contained seven plants per accession.
source: Each row plot contained seven plants per accession.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the field experiment.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing was performed for 312 accessions at Novogene (China) using short-reads Illumina NovaSeq S4 Flowcell technology.
source: Whole-genome sequencing was performed for 312 accessions at Novogene (China) using short-reads Illumina NovaSeq S4 Flowcell technology and yielded an average of 10 Gb of paired-end (PE) 2 × 150 bp reads with quality Q>30 Phred score per sample, which is equivalent to ~7× coverage of the haploid quinoa genome (~1.45 Gb).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology used in the study.

claim: Sequencing yielded an average of 10 Gb of paired-end (PE) 2 × 150 bp reads with quality Q>30 Phred score per sample, which is equivalent to ~7× coverage of the haploid quinoa genome.
source: Whole-genome sequencing was performed for 312 accessions at Novogene (China) using short-reads Illumina NovaSeq S4 Flowcell technology and yielded an average of 10 Gb of paired-end (PE) 2 × 150 bp reads with quality Q>30 Phred score per sample, which is equivalent to ~7× coverage of the haploid quinoa genome (~1.45 Gb).
evidence: This describes the sequencing output and coverage achieved in the study.

claim: All re-sequencing data are submitted to SRA under project id BioProject PRJNA673789.
source: All re-sequencing data are submitted to SRA under project id BioProject PRJNA673789.
evidence: This provides information about data availability.
